---
title: Contribute a container
---

A Dockerfile is a recipe for a container image. Check the
[container catalog](index.qmd) for an existing image before adding one.

You need Git and a GitHub account. These examples use a fictional
`exampletool` at version `1.2.3`; replace the names and versions with your own.

## Add or update a container

### 1. Create a branch

If you cannot push to Dockers2, fork it on GitHub. Use **Code** on your fork
to copy its clone URL and replace the URL below.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/CCBR/Dockers2.git
cd Dockers2
git switch -c add-exampletool
```

Run the remaining commands from the repository root.

### 2. Add a versioned Dockerfile

For a new image, create a directory and copy the template:

```sh
mkdir -p exampletool/ccbr_exampletool_1.2.3
cp template.Dockerfile exampletool/ccbr_exampletool_1.2.3/Dockerfile.v1
```

The Dockerfile's directory becomes the image name; the part after
`Dockerfile.` becomes its tag. This example produces the stable images
`nciccbr/ccbr_exampletool_1.2.3:v1` and
`ghcr.io/ccbr/ccbr_exampletool_1.2.3:v1`. Use a unique image name made of
lowercase letters and numbers separated by `.`, `_`, or `-`, and a numbered
tag such as `v1` or `v1.2.3`. A plain `Dockerfile` does not trigger an
automatic build.

Edit the copied Dockerfile:

- Choose a versioned base image and update the maintainer labels.
- Add installation commands and pin tool and dependency versions where
  possible. The template does not install your tool.
- Keep local `COPY` or `ADD` files in this directory or its subdirectories;
  this is the build context. Commit the required files.
- Do not commit credentials, private data, or unnecessary large files.

For an update, prefer a new version such as `Dockerfile.v2`: rebuilding an
existing tag can overwrite it. Keep older recipes' supporting files unchanged,
or version them too. If the image name includes the tool version, use a new
directory for a new tool version.

Images are built for `linux/amd64` by default. To support more architectures,
add a single declaration near the top of the Dockerfile, for example:

```dockerfile
# build-platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64
```

Only list platforms supported by the base image, packages, and downloaded
binaries. See the
[platform instructions](#docker-build-platforms).

### 3. Build and test locally (optional)

Local testing catches errors before CI runs, but you can skip it and test the
preview image instead (step 4). Docker is not available on GFE laptops; use
[Podman](https://podman.io/docs/installation). On macOS or Windows, start the
Podman virtual machine first:

```sh
podman machine init   # first time only
podman machine start
```

Build the example for `linux/amd64`:

```sh
podman build --platform linux/amd64 \
  --file exampletool/ccbr_exampletool_1.2.3/Dockerfile.v1 \
  --build-arg DOCKERFILE=Dockerfile.v1 \
  --build-arg BUILD_DATE="$(date -u +%Y-%m-%d_%H:%M:%S)" \
  --build-arg BUILD_TAG=v1 \
  --build-arg REPONAME=ccbr_exampletool_1.2.3 \
  --build-arg IMAGENAME=nciccbr/ccbr_exampletool_1.2.3:v1 \
  --build-arg BASEIMAGENAME=nciccbr/ccbr_ubuntu_22.04:v4 \
  --tag ccbr_exampletool_1.2.3:v1 \
  exampletool/ccbr_exampletool_1.2.3
```

If you change the template's `FROM` image, update `BASEIMAGENAME`. On Apple
silicon Macs, `linux/amd64` builds use emulation and can be slow.

Check that the tool runs and reports the expected version:

```sh
podman run --rm --platform linux/amd64 \
  localhost/ccbr_exampletool_1.2.3:v1 exampletool --version
```

Use your tool's version command; adjust it for the image's `ENTRYPOINT` if
needed. Also test a small, non-sensitive input and check the output. Save the
commands and results for your pull request.

### 4. Open a pull request

Commit and push your changes:

```sh
git add exampletool/ccbr_exampletool_1.2.3/
git commit -m "feat: add exampletool container"
git push -u origin add-exampletool
```

Open a pull request (PR) against `CCBR/Dockers2`'s `main` branch. Include the
tool and image versions, why the image is needed, and your test commands and
results. Check `build-docker-auto` in the PR checks or Actions tab; a successful
build does not replace testing the tool.

| Change | Automatic build |
|---|---|
| PR from a branch in Dockers2 | Builds and may publish `v1-dev` to Docker Hub and GHCR. |
| PR from a fork | Builds without publishing a preview. |
| Merge to `main` | Builds and publishes the stable `v1` tag. |

Preview builds can be skipped if registry tags are up to date. The `v1-dev`
tag is shared and can be overwritten; do not use it for production.

Only changes to a versioned Dockerfile or its source metadata trigger the
workflow. When updating supporting files in a PR, also change the relevant
Dockerfile in that push.

To test a published preview on Biowulf, start an interactive session and run:

```sh
module load singularity
singularity exec docker://nciccbr/ccbr_exampletool_1.2.3:v1-dev \
  exampletool --version
```

See the [Biowulf container guide](https://ccbr.github.io/HowTos/docs/containers/singularity-biowulf.html)
for setup and cache guidance. A fork PR does not publish a preview; ask a
maintainer for help.

### 5. Wait for review and merge

A maintainer will review your PR. Address any feedback and wait for a
maintainer to approve and merge it into `main`. After the merge, check that the
stable build succeeded and the tag is available in both registries.

## Publishing images

### Automatic build

The [automatic build workflow](https://github.com/CCBR/Dockers2/blob/main/.github/workflows/build-docker-auto.yml)
publishes images to Docker Hub under [`nciccbr`](https://hub.docker.com/u/nciccbr)
and to GHCR under [`ghcr.io/ccbr`](https://github.com/orgs/CCBR/packages?ecosystem=container).
For a Dockerfile named `Dockerfile.v2`, it uses these tags:

| Trigger | Tag | Publishing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pull request to `main` | `v2-dev` | Docker Hub and GHCR for same-repository PRs; fork PRs build without publishing |
| Push to an `autobuild` branch | `v2-dev` | Docker Hub and GHCR |
| Push to `main` | `v2` | Docker Hub and GHCR |

The `-dev` tag is shared by previews of the same image and version. A later
successful push can overwrite another PR's preview, so use the unsuffixed tag
for stable images. Existing registry tags are not renamed or deleted.

### Manual build

To build an image on demand, run the
[manual workflow](https://github.com/CCBR/Dockers2/blob/main/.github/workflows/build-docker-manual.yml) from the Actions
tab and select the Dockerfile. Choose `dev` for a preview or `main` for the
unsuffixed version tag; stable tags can only be published from `main`. Enable
**push** to publish to both registries; leave it unchecked to run without
publishing.

### Dispatch from another repository

To add or update an image from another repository, use the
[dispatch workflow](https://github.com/CCBR/Dockers2/blob/main/.github/workflows/build-docker-dispatch.yml).
See [Import a Dockerfile from another repository](#import-a-dockerfile-from-another-repository)
for instructions.

### Shared workflow behavior

When publishing generates a README update, the workflows use the CCBR-bot
GitHub App to merge its PR. They use the `CCBR_BOT_CLIENT_ID` variable and
`CCBR_BOT_PRIVATE_KEY` secret; fork PRs and manual builds without publishing
do not receive these credentials.

Stable publications always build rather than relying on registry timestamps,
which do not account for source-context changes. Automatic and manual stable
builds targeting the same image tag share a queue. After entering the queue,
they skip an outdated checkout if a matching image's build context has changed
on `main`; run the manual workflow again from `main` if needed. The queue holds
up to 100 pending jobs per image tag.

Other builds check the image tag in each target registry. They build if a tag
is missing, older than the Dockerfile's latest commit, missing a requested
platform, or cannot be checked; otherwise, they skip the build. The manual
workflow still checks both registries when **push** is disabled, so an
up-to-date image can skip a build-only run.

## Docker build platforms

The CI workflows read the selected Dockerfile's `build-platforms` declaration.
When the declaration is absent or empty, the image is built for `linux/amd64`.
To opt a Dockerfile into additional architectures, add a comment at the top of
the file:

```dockerfile
# build-platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64
FROM ubuntu:26.04
```

List platforms as comma-separated `os/arch[/variant]` values, using any
platform supported by `docker buildx` (for example, `linux/arm/v7` or
`linux/ppc64le`). Duplicates, malformed values, multiple declarations, and
platforms the base image does not provide fail the build rather than silently
publishing an incomplete image. For manual builds, a nonempty `platforms` input
overrides the declaration and uses the same validation; leave it blank to use
the Dockerfile's selection. Enable **push** when manually building multiple
platforms.

Only declare a platform after confirming the base image, packages, downloaded
binaries, and other dependencies support it. Multi-platform builds use
emulation on GitHub's x86 runners and can take significantly longer.
Published images include the requested platforms; your local container engine
(Docker, Podman, Apptainer) selects the matching one automatically.

## Import a Dockerfile from another repository

For a Dockerfile maintained elsewhere, use **Actions > build-docker-dispatch >
[Run workflow](https://github.com/CCBR/Dockers2/actions/workflows/build-docker-dispatch.yml)**
in Dockers2. You need permission to run the workflow, and it must be able to
access the source repository. Enter the source `OWNER/REPO`, ref, Dockerfile
path, lowercase image name, and a tag such as `v1`. Use a source tag or
commit; the image tag can be at most 124 characters, leaving room for the
`-dev` suffix within Docker's 128-character tag limit.

The source repository root must be the Dockerfile's intended build context.
Before running, check for credentials, private data, and unnecessary large
files: the workflow copies and commits the entire checkout except `.git`.

The workflow records the exact source commit in `.Dockerfile.<tag>.source.json`
next to the Dockerfile and publishes a `-dev` preview to Docker Hub and GHCR.
After a successful build, it opens or updates a PR to `main` containing the
Dockerfile, metadata, and copied context. Review the copied files and metadata,
and test the preview; merging the PR triggers the stable build.

Automatic and manual builds use the checked-in snapshot without needing access
to the source repository. Changes to the metadata also trigger a rebuild; keep
it alongside the Dockerfile. Older dispatched Dockerfiles that do not include
their source context must be dispatched again if they need files from the
source repository. Rerun the dispatch when the source changes.

For on-demand builds of recipes already in Dockers2, see the
[manual build instructions](#manual-build).
A build-only run can still be skipped if the registry tags are up to date.
